CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 156 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 10/05/2026 - PAGE 10F 2

THE OKLAHOMAN #2 FILE

GUEST | Opinion This piece expresses the views of its author(s), separate from those of this publication.

OK utility customers have rare legal rights
worth defending | Opinion

Bob Anthony Guest columnist
Sept. 30, 2026, 6:30 a.m. CT

As they grapple with legitimate issues involving data centers, water, transmission lines,
an aluminum smelter, utility rates, the environment and basic affordability, Oklahoma
utility customers are fortunate that the framers of the Oklahoma Constitution provided
them with some of the strongest consumer protections of any state in the nation. They
should immediately be skeptical of any effort to curtail ratepayers’ legal rights —
especially a constitutional convention seeking to amend them.

Written at the turn of the 20th century by trust-busting leaders seeking to rein in the
power of monopolies, Article 9 of the Oklahoma Constitution establishes a state
Corporation Commission with more than just the power to regulate. Commissioners have
mandatory constitutional duties, including “to inspect the books and papers” of regulated
companies, to set rates that are “reasonable and just,” to “correct abuses” and to “prevent
unjust discrimination.” That includes making sure that existing customers don’t unfairly
pay for new generation, transmission and other infrastructure upgrades required to serve
data centers and other large-load customers as they come online.

And in case the Corporation Commission fails to do its duty, the Constitution gives any
“aggrieved” utility customer the right to appeal a commission utility order directly to the
Oklahoma Supreme Court.

In every such appeal, Article 9, Section 20 requires the Supreme Court to determine
whether the commission’s order is sustained by the law and substantial evidence. The
court is also required to determine whether the commission has regularly pursued its
authority — not just, did it keep within the limits of its powers, but did the commission

fulfill its regulatory duties required by the constitution. Thus, any individual ratepayer
can hold the Corporation Commission accountable.

Appeal of certain commission orders “shall be to the Supreme Court only” and “such
appeal shall be of right,” and I believe ratepayers are entitled to due process of law,
including notice and hearing. Furthermore, the Oklahoma Constitution states, “All such
appeals, affecting rates, charges, practices, rules or regulations of any public utility, or
any public service corporation, or any individual, person, firm, corporation, receiver or
trustee engaged in the public utility business, shall have precedence upon the docket of
the Supreme Court, irrespective of its place of session, next after habeas corpus cases, to
the end that a plain, speedy, and efficient remedy may be afforded the parties to such
appeals.”

Some may think there have been too many ratepayer-led commission utility appeals in
recent years. I disagree. The attorney general has a statutory duty to represent the
collective interests of utility customers in commission utility cases, but by my count, the
last attorney general to bring an appeal of a commission utility case on behalf of
consumers was Susan Loving in 1992!

When Corporation Commissioners and the attorney general both fail to do their duty to
protect the public, aggrieved utility customers should exercise their constitutional right to
ask the Supreme Court to step in. The solution to having too many Supreme Court
appeals is not to eliminate that constitutional consumer protection; the solution is for
elected officials to do their duty and follow the law.

In 1989, some constitutional convention advocates proposed to dramatically alter Article
g. I opposed it then, and I would oppose it again today. Before considering any changes to
our Constitution, Oklahomans should make sure they understand the specific legal
protections that currently exist to protect customers from monopoly public utilities as
well as to ensure an open regulatory process with just results in the public interest.

Bob Anthony was an Oklahoma Corporation Commissioner from 1989-2025.
